item.title: Numerical Testing of an EOS Implementation
item.description:
Working with an equation of state means differentiating it, repeatedly. You need pressure as a derivative of Helmholtz energy, chemical potentials as derivatives with respect to composition, fugacity coefficients built from those, and second derivatives on top for anything that solves by Newton’s method. The expressions are considerably worse than polynomials, and in most production code they are derived by hand and then coded — autodiff costs a factor of several per evaluation, and a flash calculation calls these functions millions of times.

Both steps can go wrong, and the failure is quiet. A derivative that is wrong by half a percent produces numbers that look entirely plausible. Your flash calculation still converges — just more slowly, or to the wrong answer near a phase boundary, or not at all at the one state point you needed.

What makes this tractable is that you do not need a second implementation to check against, and you do not need symbolic algebra. You can check a derivative against the only thing you are sure of: the function it claims to differentiate.

Where and come from

Take any function and perturb its argument to . A Taylor expansion says exactly what happens:

Now truncate Equation 1 at successive orders and ask how wrong you are each time. That is the whole idea, and both and come straight out of it.

Truncate after the first term. Pretend does not change at all, so . The error you make is everything you discarded:

Truncate after the second term. Now use the derivative you are testing. The error left over is:

So and are the same kind of object — truncation errors of the same series — measured one order apart. That is the entire construction.

Two observations before going further.

Neither is zero, and neither is supposed to be. Chasing a small is the wrong instinct; what carries the information is the rate at which each one vanishes as shrinks.

And note the asymmetry. has a leading term plus corrections, so for small you can legitimately drop everything after . cannot be simplified the same way — its leading term is the first surviving term, and there is nothing larger to compare it against.

Only one of these quantities contains your derivative. is computed from two calls to and nothing else, so it cannot be wrong. is the only place your claim enters, which is why it is the one that tests it.

Why the slope is 2

Work it through on , where and everything is visible:

For small the quadratic term in Equation 4 is negligible beside the linear one, so . Take logarithms of both:

Here is held fixed and only varies, so is a constant. Eliminate between Equation 6 and Equation 7:

A straight line of slope 2. Not approximately, not asymptotically — this is what the algebra gives, for a correctly coded derivative.

Why it fails loudly when the derivative is wrong

Suppose your code returns instead of the true value. Then Equation 3 becomes

The leading term is now first order in , exactly like . So and the slope collapses to 1.

This is why the test is sharp. However small is, eventually beats , so the wrong first-order term always wins in the limit. A tiny error does not produce a slope of 1.99 — it produces a slope of 1. You are reading a rate, not a magnitude, and there is no tolerance to tune.

The general case

Nothing above needed . Dividing Equation 3 by the square of Equation 2, the factors cancel:

so for any twice-differentiable ,

Slope 2 always; the intercept depends on the function and on where you evaluate it. For that intercept is , which is Equation 8 again.

The split matters: the intercept is what you would need to know the function to predict, and the slope is not. That is why the test is built on the slope.

Checking it on functions you can differentiate by hand

Two functions first, including one wrong derivative for contrast. For the series does not terminate — — so the correction in Equation 10 is visible at large steps and fades as the step shrinks.

Two correct derivatives give 2. A five percent error gives 1. Nothing lands in between, and the gap widens as the step shrinks rather than narrowing.

Five percent is an arbitrary choice, so the obvious question is whether the slope also reports how wrong the derivative is. It does not.

Every column converges on 1, and the larger errors arrive sooner — at the coarsest step a 50% error already reads 0.9980 while a 1% error is still at 0.9275. So the slope answers whether the derivative is wrong, not by how much. That is the useful behaviour for a test: a one percent error is as detectable as a catastrophic one, and you do not need to guess the size of the bug in advance to choose a step size.

Does it hold generally?

Two cases prove little, and Equation 10 claims something about every twice-differentiable function — including the intercept. A wider sweep:

Growth rates from to , a sign-changing second derivative, a product needing the chain rule. Every slope is 2 to four decimals and every intercept matches Equation 10 to five. That is the case for trusting the method on something you cannot differentiate by hand.

Measuring the slope properly

Each perturbation produces exactly one and one , so a series of step sizes produces a series of points — one point per step. Writing

a run over five values of gives five pairs , and the slope you are testing is the slope of the line through them.

Why two points is the minimum

A single perturbation gives a single point, and a single point has no slope — infinitely many lines pass through it.

It is tempting to think the ratio would do. It would, if the line passed through the origin. It does not: Equation 10 puts the intercept at , which for the worked example below is about 4.01. Taking the ratio anyway, on that same data:
1e-02 1.1717 −5.1997 −4.4377
1e-03 −1.1324 −9.8044 8.6580
1e-04 −3.4351 −14.4095 4.1947
1e-05 −5.7377 −19.0149 3.3140

Not one of them is near 2, and they do not even agree with each other. The intercept is responsible for the whole mess, and it is not optional — it carries real information, since Equation 10 predicts it in closed form.

Two points remove the problem, because the unknown intercept cancels.

Do not assume the slope — it is the thing being measured. Call it , leave the intercept as , and write the relation at two step sizes and :

Two equations, two unknowns. Subtracting eliminates whatever its value and leaves on its own:

This matters for the logic of the test. Equation 13 measures from the data without assuming anything about it. Theory then predicts what it should be: if the derivative is correct, if it is not. Comparing the two is the test. Had we written in Equation 12 we would have assumed the answer and learned nothing.

Equation 13 is what the slope columns in every table here compute. Each value belongs to a pair of rows, not to a single row — which is why those columns are labelled by an interval and why the last row has no entry.

So two points is the minimum. They determine a unique line, so they fix as well as — back-substituting recovers it. Equation 13 simply avoids needing it. That is a convenience, not a limitation.

What two points cannot give you is any evidence that the relation is linear in the first place. A line through two points fits them exactly, with zero residual, so there is nothing left over to tell you whether the slope is stable. Five perturbations give you that, and stability across the range is what locates the round-off floor.

Fitting all of them at once

Reading the slope a pair at a time is fine for seeing the trend, but each value uses only two of your points and depends on which pair you picked. Least squares uses all of them:

The subscript indexes the perturbations — one term per step size — and the overbars are means over that series.

Where Equation 14 comes from

It is ordinary linear least squares, and it is worth seeing that this form is not a rearrangement of the familiar one — it is what the normal equations give directly. Fitting means choosing and to minimise

Differentiating with respect to the intercept and setting it to zero,

so the fitted line passes through the centroid of the data. Differentiating with respect to the slope,

and substituting Equation 16 into Equation 17 gives

which is Equation 14 solved for . The more commonly quoted is the same number, obtained by adding and subtracting terms that vanish because deviations from a mean sum to zero.

One detail worth noticing: the intercept is free here, not pinned to zero. That is deliberate — Equation 10 predicts a non-zero intercept, and forcing the line through the origin would bias the slope.

The worked example

SRK for a methane–ethane binary, as a residual Helmholtz function. With

the residual Helmholtz energy and the composition derivative under test are

where , , and .

Equation 19 is the reason this post exists. Four terms, each arriving by a different path through the chain rule, and no way to tell by looking whether it is right.

R, T, V = 8.314462618, 300.0, 500.0      # J/mol/K, K, cm3
Tc  = [190.56, 305.32]                    # K
Pc  = [4.599e6, 4.872e6]                  # Pa
w   = [0.011, 0.099]
n   = [0.6, 0.4]                          # mol
k12 = 0.01

b  = [8.664e4 * (tc * R) / pc for tc, pc in zip(Tc, Pc)]
ac = [4.2747e5 * ((R * tc) ** 2) / pc for tc, pc in zip(Tc, Pc)]
m  = [0.48 + 1.574 * z - 0.175 * z * z for z in w]
al = [(1 + mi * (1 - math.sqrt(T / tc))) ** 2 for mi, tc in zip(m, Tc)]
a  = [aci * ali for aci, ali in zip(ac, al)]
aij = [[a[0], math.sqrt(a[0] * a[1]) * (1 - k12)],
       [math.sqrt(a[0] * a[1]) * (1 - k12), a[1]]]

def A_res(nv):
    B = sum(ni * bi for ni, bi in zip(nv, b))
    D = sum(nv[i] * nv[j] * aij[i][j] for i in range(2) for j in range(2))
    return -sum(nv) * R * T * math.log(1 - B / V) - D * math.log(1 + B / V) / B

B = sum(ni * bi for ni, bi in zip(n, b))
D = sum(n[i] * n[j] * aij[i][j] for i in range(2) for j in range(2))
g, f = math.log(1 - B / V), math.log(1 + B / V) / B
g_B  = -1 / (V - B)
f_V  = -1 / (V * (V + B))
f_B  = -(f + V * f_V) / B
D1   = 2 * (aij[0][0] * n[0] + aij[0][1] * n[1])

A_n1 = -R * T * g - sum(n) * R * T * g_B * b[0] - D1 * f - D * f_B * b[0]

print(f"A_res = {A_res(n):.6f} J")
print(f"A_n1  = {A_n1:.6f} J/mol")
A_res = -406.946593 J
A_n1  = -537.005260 J/mol

Perturbing a mole number

One practical change from the theory above. Rather than a fixed , perturb relatively: , so . Nothing in the derivation cares — was arbitrary — but it means carries the same meaning whether a variable is of order or , which matters once you start testing across the phase diagram.

falls by ten per row; by one hundred. The slope column reads 2. Equation 19 is correct.

F1 = [math.log(abs(r[1])) for r in rows]
F2 = [math.log(abs(r[2])) for r in rows]

def ls_slope(f1, f2):
    m1, m2 = sum(f1) / len(f1), sum(f2) / len(f2)
    return (sum(a * (b_ - m2) for a, b_ in zip(f1, f2))
            / sum(a * (a - m1) for a in f1))

print(f"all five points    slope = {ls_slope(F1, F2):.6f}")
print(f"drop p = 1e-6      slope = {ls_slope(F1[:4], F2[:4]):.6f}")
print(f"p = 1e-2 to 1e-4   slope = {ls_slope(F1[:3], F2[:3]):.6f}")
all five points    slope = 2.000636
drop p = 1e-6      slope = 1.999492
p = 1e-2 to 1e-4   slope = 1.999146

Where it stops working

Look at the last row of the table. The slope column drifts, and the least-squares fit over all five points sits slightly above 2 while the fit over the clean range sits just below.

That is round-off, not a wrong derivative. At we extract a quantity of order from a difference of numbers of order — thirteen significant figures, against the sixteen or so double precision carries. Most of the precision is consumed by cancellation before Equation 3 even subtracts.

This is the finite-difference tradeoff, and the consequence is worth stating plainly: shrinking does not sharpen the test indefinitely. Truncation error falls as the step shrinks; round-off error rises. The usable window here runs from about to , and you find it by looking for where the slope is flat rather than by assuming smaller is better.

What a failure looks like

Suppose the last term of Equation 19, , were wrong by one percent.

A_n1_bad = A_n1 - 0.01 * (D * f_B * b[0])
bad = [(p, E1, E1 - A_n1_bad * n[0] * p) for p, E1, _ in rows]

print("| $p$ range | slope, correct | slope, 1% error |")
print("| --- | --- | --- |")
for k in range(len(rows) - 1):
    good = (math.log(abs(rows[k][2] / rows[k+1][2]))
            / math.log(abs(rows[k][1] / rows[k+1][1])))
    poor = (math.log(abs(bad[k][2] / bad[k+1][2]))
            / math.log(abs(bad[k][1] / bad[k+1][1])))
    print(f"| {rows[k][0]:.0e} to {rows[k+1][0]:.0e} | {good:.4f} | {poor:.4f} |")
range slope, correct slope, 1% error
1e-02 to 1e-03 1.9984 1.6216
1e-03 to 1e-04 1.9998 1.1672
1e-04 to 1e-05 2.0001 1.0209
1e-05 to 1e-06 2.0049 1.0021

The correct column holds at 2; the broken one collapses toward 1 as the step shrinks, exactly as the five percent error on did. One wrong term out of four, under one percent of the total value, and the test reads it off unambiguously.

You would not have caught that by checking the number looked reasonable.

When slope 1 is not a bug

One case breaks that reading. If the derivative you are testing happens to be zero at your test point, vanishes, Equation 3 collapses to , and the slope is 1 however good your code is:

and are not zero here — they are equal, both of order , because still changes quadratically even where its slope does not. Plotting against is then plotting a quantity against itself, so the slope is 1 for a trivial reason and the derivative was never tested at all.

This is not contrived for an equation of state: vanishes on the spinodal, and residual properties vanish in the ideal-gas limit. The tell is the ratio. pinned at exactly 1 means the derivative returned zero, where a genuine relative error gives a constant instead. Report the ratio beside the slope, and move the test point when it reads 1.

“But my derivatives come from a computer”

Worth answering before you build any of this into a test suite.

If you differentiate with autodiff — dual numbers, JAX, reverse mode — the derivative is generated from the function’s own code and is correct to machine precision by construction. The algebra-slip risk genuinely disappears. So is the test pointless?

No, and the clearest evidence is that the autodiff ecosystem ships this exact test. PyTorch’s torch.autograd.gradcheck validates analytical gradients against finite differences, and is the documented way to verify a custom autograd.Function. JAX has check_grads. Both exist because the computer did the differentiation and somebody still wanted proof.

The reason is that the test never asks where the derivative came from. It asks whether your derivative code is consistent with your function code, and that is the same question however the derivative was produced. What changes is what a slope of 1 tells you:

Derivative from What slope 1 means
Hand derivation An algebra slip, or a typo in the code
Symbolic algebra, retyped A transcription error
Autodiff A branch, an internal solver, a custom rule, or the wrong variable
Any of them, months later The function changed and the derivative did not

Where autodiff actually breaks on EOS code

The interesting failures are not in the differentiation. They are in the assumptions around it, and equation-of-state code is unusually rich in them.

Branches. Which cubic root is the liquid? That is an if. Autodiff differentiates the branch taken and tells you nothing about the switch — and near a phase boundary the switch is exactly where you need the derivative to be right.

Internal iterative solves. If the function solves for volume by Newton iteration, naive autodiff differentiates through the iterations instead of applying the implicit function theorem. That is correct only if the iteration converged tightly, and silently wrong otherwise.

Custom derivative rules. The moment you hand-write one for speed you are back to hand-derivation, with less scrutiny, because it looks like autodiff.

Splines and lookup tables. You get the interpolant’s derivative, which is not the property’s derivative.

A symbolic package has a different weakness. It hands you a correct expression, and then a human retypes it as code, splits it across intermediate variables, and reuses a term computed earlier. The derivation was right; the implementation is not.

The reason that never goes away

Someone swaps the correlation, or makes temperature dependent, updates Equation 18 and forgets Equation 19. However the derivative was produced originally, the two code paths have now drifted apart, and this test is what notices.

That makes it a regression test, and regression tests do not care how correct the code was on the day it was written.

What it does not check

It verifies your derivative against your function, not against your intent. Ask for when you wanted , test the same wrong thing, and it passes with slope 2 — consistently differentiating the wrong quantity. The test tells you the two code paths agree. Whether they are the pair you meant is still yours to get right.

Using it in practice

  • Test at several states. A derivative can be right in the vapour region and wrong near the critical point, where behaves differently.
  • Work outwards. Verify first derivatives before second. A second derivative checked against a wrong first derivative tells you nothing.
  • Perturb relatively, so one means the same thing for every variable.
  • Find the flat window before trusting a number, rather than assuming the smallest step is best.
  • Use the free checks too. Mixed second derivatives should be symmetric, , which costs one comparison and no perturbation at all. Euler’s theorem gives another: should reproduce a quantity you can compute directly.
  • Assert the slope, not the table. Check that the fitted slope from Equation 14 is within tolerance of 2 across the clean window, and the whole thing runs in CI with nobody reading anything.

The idea generalises past equations of state. Any time you differentiate something by hand and then implement it, you have made two independent claims and verified neither. This checks both against the one thing you are sure of.

Reference

The / construction and the slope-2 criterion are a standard technique for verifying hand-derived analytical derivatives against finite differences. The SRK Helmholtz formulation in terms of , , and is standard; the worked binary, the multi-function sweep and the round-off analysis are my own.

item.title: Why AI Chat Math Won’t Paste Into Word, and What Actually Travels on the Clipboard
item.description:
Copy a formula out of ChatGPT and paste it into Word and you get one of three disappointments: a picture you cannot edit, a line of raw \frac{a}{b}, or a row of mangled symbols. None of them is a Word equation.

That is not Word being obtuse. The formula on screen was never an equation, and the thing Word wants is a format no chat site produces. This post is about what sits on each side of that gap, and what has to go on the clipboard to bridge it.

A formula on a web page is not a formula

Nothing in a web page is an equation. A chat site renders math with a JavaScript library, almost always MathJax or KaTeX, and what lands in the DOM is one of:

  • SVG. MathJax’s SVG output draws each glyph as vector paths. Visually perfect, semantically nothing. Copy it and you have copied a drawing.
  • Styled HTML. MathJax’s CommonHTML output and KaTeX build the formula from spans with careful CSS. What looks like a fraction bar is a <span> with a border.
  • An image. A few sites still render server-side to PNG.

The visual layer is a dead end in all three cases. What rescues the situation is that the libraries also leave the semantics in the page, out of sight. KaTeX emits a hidden MathML copy next to the visual one; MathJax ships an Assistive MathML extension that, in its own words, “inserts hidden MathML for the usual output renderers.” And MathML has a slot for the original source:

<annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{RT}{V_m - b}</annotation>

So the LaTeX you typed is usually still on the page, one layer down. Finding it reliably is harder than it sounds: the attribute names, the element structure and even whether the hidden copy exists at all vary by renderer, by renderer version, and by how a given site configures it. But the principle holds everywhere. Anything that moves chat math somewhere useful works from that hidden semantic layer, not from the pixels on top.

What Word stores

Word’s native equation format is OMML, Office Math Markup Language. An equation inside a .docx is a tree of m: elements in word/document.xml, in the namespace

http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/officeDocument/2006/math

Nothing on a web page produces OMML. That is the problem in one sentence.

Route 1: linear format, typed by hand

Word accepts an equation written on one line and then “built up” into two dimensions. It supports two linear formats, and the difference matters: UnicodeMath, Microsoft’s own compact notation, and LaTeX.

Alt + = opens an equation field; type or paste the linear source; Ctrl + = builds it up. Ctrl + Shift + = goes back.

Two limits before you rely on it. Microsoft describes LaTeX input as new to Microsoft 365 subscribers, so on a perpetual licence do not assume it is there. And Word’s LaTeX is a dialect: \begin{} and \end{} are unsupported, so environments do not work and you write \matrix{a & b \\ c & d} instead, while \eqarray, \Middle, \ldiv and \dsmash are not supported at all.

This route works, it needs no tooling, and it does not scale past a few formulas.

Route 2: hand Word its own format on the clipboard

This is the route that actually scales, and the one people are surprised exists.

When you paste into Word, Word does not read the plain-text flavour of the clipboard. It reads the text/html flavour — and it reads it as Word’s own HTML, a dialect that has carried Office-specific markup since the days of “Save as Web Page”. Word understands OMML embedded there, and it understands markup addressed to itself that every other application is required to skip.

That second property is what makes the whole thing work. A single clipboard payload can carry a real OMML equation for Word and readable LaTeX for everything else, and each reader takes its own branch. Paste into Word and you get a native equation; paste the same clipboard into a plain text editor and you get $\frac{RT}{V_m - b}$.

The practical consequence is that a tool doing this well is not “converting LaTeX to Word”. It is walking the page’s MathML into OMML, wrapping that in a Word-flavoured HTML payload, and writing text/html and text/plain together so the paste degrades sensibly wherever it lands. Getting the conversion right across real-world formulas — matrices, cases, multi-line alignments, over- and under-braces — is where the actual work is.

Route 3: write the file

Skip the clipboard and generate the .docx yourself. A Word file is a zip of XML; the math goes in under the officeDocument/2006/math namespace and the document body under wordprocessingml/2006/main. Most work, most control, and the only route that handles a whole chat transcript at once rather than one formula at a time.

Why Word on the web is different

Word in a browser cannot accept a pasted equation from any application, because a browser tab never receives the rich clipboard payload the desktop app does. The conditional-comment trick needs Word itself reading the clipboard, and in the web app there is no Word reading the clipboard.

The workaround is Route 1, explicitly: Insert → Equation, paste the linear source into the box at the top of the panel, press Space, insert. It works, and it is also where the dialect limits bite hardest, because matrices, cases and multi-line equations are exactly what that box cannot build.

PowerPoint, Excel, Google

One line in Microsoft’s documentation explains a great deal of confusion:

All other Office applications support only UnicodeMath.

PowerPoint, Excel and Outlook do not take LaTeX input. A workflow built on pasting LaTeX into Word does not transfer to a slide deck, which is why getting a formula into PowerPoint means OMML or an image.

Google Docs and Slides have no equation format worth targeting at all. There a high-resolution image is not a compromise, it is the correct answer.

Picking a route

Route Result Where it works Main cost
Linear, typed Native, editable Word desktop; LaTeX needs 365 Manual; dialect gaps
OMML in HTML clipboard Native, editable Word, PowerPoint desktop Must generate OMML
Generated .docx Native, editable Anywhere Word opens Most work
Image Not editable Everywhere, incl. Google Fixed resolution

There is no single format that is both easy to produce and universally accepted, which is the whole reason this is annoying.

The tool

I write thermodynamics, and a post like Thermodynamic Potentials Applied for Equations of State carries over two hundred equations. Rebuilding those by hand in Word for a report was not something I was willing to keep doing, so I built TeXbridge, a Chrome and Edge extension that does the above: reads the hidden semantic layer, converts to OMML, and picks a target format based on where the formula is going. If a site renders something it handles badly, there is a support page and FAQ.

The mechanism is worth knowing either way. If you understand that the LaTeX is hiding in an annotation element, and that Word reads text/html with a conditional comment in it, you can get a formula where it needs to go by hand.

Sources

Linear formats, the Alt + = and Ctrl + = mechanics, the Microsoft 365 note and the unsupported LaTeX keywords come from Microsoft’s Linear format equations using UnicodeMath and LaTeX in Word. The assistive MathML behaviour is described in the MathJax MathML documentation. Checked 30 October 2026.

item.title: Thermodynamic Potentials Applied for Equations of State
item.description:
Equation of State of an Ideal Gas

In Equation 1, the term acts as an arbitrary reference volume, which corresponds to a specific but unknown reference Helmholtz free energy, (where ). To see how this plays out mathematically, let’s look at the most basic example using the ideal-gas equation of state:

By substituting this into the fundamental volume derivative of the Helmholtz energy and performing the integration, we get:

While Equation 3 allows us to calculate changes in Helmholtz free energy, it only provides the difference between states—we still do not know the absolute values of or . If we differentiate Equation 3 with respect to temperature and apply the canonical entropy relationship, we arrive at a familiar expression for entropy:

Notice that in Equation 4, the temperature remains constant between the state of interest and the reference state.

If we were to differentiate Equation 3 with respect to volume instead, we would simply get the ideal gas law (). However, differentiating with respect to the number of moles yields the change in chemical potential:

These relationships highlight a major limitation: an equation of state (EOS) is not very helpful for calculating absolute thermodynamic properties. For instance, Equation 4 doesn’t give us the actual overarching formula for entropy; it only shows how entropy differences relate to changes in volume and composition. The same limitation applies to Equation 5 regarding chemical potential.

For now, we can set this limitation aside. Moving forward, we will apply this exact same mathematical framework to much more powerful equations of state. To make those models work, we will introduce the concept of a residual property—which is simply the mathematical difference between a property calculated from our advanced real-gas model and that same property calculated for an ideal gas.

Soave–Redlich–Kwong Equation of State

Now, let’s apply the integration specified in Equation 3 to a more advanced model: the Soave-Redlich-Kwong equation of state (SRK EOS).

In this expression, the parameters and are typically dependent on both temperature and composition. Notice that we have structured the SRK EOS here as a function of , , and the total number of moles (), rather than using mole fractions. We have also kept the unit choices generalized, consistent with our earlier discussions.

Finally, because it will be necessary for future calculations, we can determine the absolute minimum possible volume for the SRK EOS simply by inspecting the denominator of the first term:

Before we dive into the integration, it helps to algebraically rewrite the SRK EOS into a form that is easier to integrate:

Applying the integration from Equation 3 to this new form yields:

At this point, we could try to push forward, but we run into the exact same roadblock we saw with Equation 3: we still don’t know the absolute value of for an SRK fluid at an arbitrary reference volume.

However, we can bypass this issue by comparing our SRK fluid calculations directly to those of an ideal gas. If we subtract the ideal gas result (Equation 3) from our SRK result (Equation 9), we get:

At first glance, it might look like we just mashed two underdefined equations together. But remember two crucial facts: first, the conditions apply equally to both the SRK fluid and the Ideal Gas. Second, we have complete freedom to choose our reference volume, , however is most convenient.

If we define to approach infinity (), we are simulating an infinitely expanded gas. Because any valid, useful equation of state must trend toward ideal gas behavior at infinite volume, we can safely conclude that as , the real fluid properties converge with the ideal gas properties (). Additionally, under this mathematical limit, terms like simply approach 1.

Note

As , the term becomes negligible compared to the infinitely expanding volume, causing the fraction to approach unity:

Alternatively, expressed as a simple directional trend:

By applying this infinite-volume reference state, Equation 10 beautifully simplifies to:

The left-hand side of Equation 13 provides us with the formal definition of the Residual Helmholtz Free Energy:

It is crucial to understand the conceptual leap that led us to Equation 13, particularly how specific terms algebraically cancel out as our reference volume approaches infinity (). Furthermore, the core definition of any Residual Property strictly requires that both the real fluid and the Ideal Gas (IG) reference state share the exact same temperature (), volume (), and composition (). By substituting residual properties into our earlier definitions, we obtain the following relationships:

However, Equations 15 through 17 do not magically solve all our problems. While we can differentiate Equation 13 with respect to , , or to generate residual properties, we still cannot determine the absolute property of the SRK fluid without knowing the corresponding property of the ideal gas.

Fortunately, we do know the pressure for both the ideal gas and the SRK fluid, which allows us to completely solve for the volume derivative, .

Regarding composition (), we will see in the next section that if we can successfully formulate the ideal gas chemical potential (), we can then derive a highly useful expression for the chemical potential () of the SRK fluid (and other equations of state).

Finally, when it comes to temperature (), we will discover that for a massive category of thermodynamic calculations, we actually do not need to know the absolute ideal gas entropy. In practice, those terms frequently end up canceling out algebraically when we assemble the final equations.

The Chemical Potential of an Ideal Gas

Let’s start from the canonical derivative relation for the ideal gas Helmholtz free energy (Equation 18):

Substituting the ideal gas law, (Equation 2), yields:

Integrating this expression with respect to volume (), while keeping temperature () and the composition vector () constant, gives us:

Notice that Equation 1 is now composed entirely of state functions. This introduces internal energy () as a thermodynamic potential, indicating that is fundamentally a function of entropy, volume, and the number of moles. While it is mathematically possible to express internal energy using temperature and volume instead, the resulting equation loses its compact elegance—a natural mathematical framing referred to as a canonical relationship.

However, applying Equation 1 directly requires functional models that relate variables like , , and back to , , and . Because such models are rare and typically impractical for standard chemical engineering applications, it is often more useful to mathematically eliminate entropy as an independent variable. We do this using an operation called a Legendre transformation:

Expanding the differential yields:

Canceling out the terms gives us the transformed potential:

We might recognize the left side of Equation 2 as the definition of the Helmholtz free energy ():

If you haven’t encountered Helmholtz free energy before, do not worry; the key takeaway at this stage is recognizing that we have defined a new property (distinct from internal energy) that acts as a canonical function of temperature, volume, and composition ():

From a multivariable calculus perspective, this total differential allows us to extract the following partial derivatives:

For our current purposes, Equation 6 is the most crucial. If we have a pressure-explicit equation of state—meaning we know pressure as a function of , , and —we can easily calculate differences in Helmholtz free energy by integrating:

An even more commonly recognized potential is the Gibbs free energy. We can derive it by applying another Legendre transformation to Equation 4, this time swapping out volume in favor of pressure as our independent variable:

Expanding this and substituting our previous enthalpy definitions yields the fundamental relation for Gibbs free energy ():

Although Gibbs energy is ideal for constant T and P problems, it is clumsy as an overarching computational framework. Most equations of state solve for P(T, V), not V(T, P), because volume is multi-valued across phase transitions—such as water at 100°C and 1atm, where liquid and vapor share identical pressures. Practical computational thermodynamics therefore depends on working with other potentials, notably Helmholtz energy, to avoid root-finding ambiguities.

Why Gibbs Energy Is Difficult to Integrate Directly from an EOS

While Gibbs free energy might feel more intuitive when dealing with constant temperature () and pressure () problems like phase equilibrium and reactions, directly calculating by integrating an equation of state presents significant mathematical hurdles.

The fundamental differential expression for requires us to integrate volume with respect to pressure:

The problem is that standard equations of state (like cubic EOS models) are fundamentally cubic in volume (). This means it is impossible to algebraically rearrange them into a clean, single-valued explicit function of the form .

Furthermore, if you are working within the two-phase region, the function becomes multi-valued—it simultaneously yields roots for the liquid phase, the vapor phase, and a mechanically unstable state. This multi-valued nature makes integrating directly along the path incredibly cumbersome.

Helmholtz energy (), however, offers a trivial workaround. Integrating the expression is straightforward because pressure () is explicitly and uniquely defined as an algebraic function of volume () across the entire thermodynamic domain. Once you have calculated , you can instantly recover the Gibbs energy simply by adding the term.

1. Volume Is Not a Mathematical Function of Pressure

Strictly speaking, for a mathematical relationship to be considered a true function (), every input must map to exactly one output.

However, for fluids operating below their critical point, defining the temperature () and pressure () does not guarantee a unique volume:

Phase Coexistence: Think about water boiling at 100°C and 1 atm. At those exact conditions, the system could be a purely saturated liquid (), a purely saturated vapor (), or any two-phase mixture in between.

Analytic Equations of State: When using models like Peng-Robinson or Soave-Redlich-Kwong, setting and within the two-phase envelope results in a cubic polynomial that produces three real roots:

  1. A small root (representing the liquid-like volume).
  2. A large root (representing the vapor-like volume).
  3. An intermediate root that is mechanically unstable (where ).

Because is multi-valued in these scenarios, it is impossible to express it as a clean, explicit, single-valued algebraic function of the form .

2. The Computational Bottleneck with Gibbs Energy

To compute changes in Gibbs energy directly from mechanical variables, the fundamental math requires us to integrate volume over pressure

Because volume is multi-valued across phase transitions, trying to evaluate forces us to trace theoretical paths through unstable van der Waals loops or manually enforce equal-area Maxwell constructions. This complexity makes direct path integration of Gibbs energy highly impractical for computational models.

3. Why the Helmholtz Framework Resolves This

While volume is not a single-valued function of pressure, the reverse is incredibly convenient: pressure is always a single-valued function of volume.

Because of this mathematical reality, if you specify the temperature () and volume (), calculating the pressure requires only a single, straightforward evaluation of the equation of state (EOS). This leads to two major advantages in computational thermodynamics:

Seamless Integration: The integral used to calculate the residual Helmholtz free energy is continuous, single-valued, and analytically integrable across the entire fluid domain (smoothly covering both liquid and vapor phases without unstable loops):

How Thermodynamics Engines Actually Work: Because of these mathematical advantages, modern computational thermodynamics engines compute all their core variables—including residual properties, fugacity coefficients (), and chemical potentials—entirely within the Helmholtz domain. When a user actually requests a result at a specific constant temperature and pressure (), the solver first finds the volumetric roots () at that given pressure, evaluates , and then simply recovers the Gibbs free energy algebraically at the very end:

item.title: From the First Law to the Fundamental Relation
item.description:
First Law of Thermodynamics for a closed system, starting from the universal principle of conservation of energy.

1. Total Energy Conservation

Because the universe is isolated, the sum of all energy changes must equal zero: energy cannot be created or destroyed:

The universe is divided into two parts: the System (Sys, the region of interest) and the Surroundings (Surr, everything else).

The total energy of any body or region consists of:

  • : macroscopic kinetic energy (movement of the center of mass)
  • : macroscopic potential energy (position in external fields, like gravity).
  • : microscopic internal energy (molecular vibrations, rotations, electronic states, intermolecular forces)

2. Practical Approximations and Boundary Transfers

Neglecting macroscopic motion of the system: In most chemical and physical systems (e.g., a beaker, reactor, or piston), the system as a whole does not undergo changes in bulk elevation or bulk velocity, meaning and . Therefore, the only energy change occurring inside the system is internal energy: .

Energy transfer across the boundary: Modeling the entire surrounding universe is practically impossible. Instead of tracking what happens inside the surroundings, thermodynamics tracks the energy crossing the boundary between the system and surroundings:

  • (Heat): Energy transferred due to a temperature difference.
  • (Work): Energy transferred through mechanical, electrical, or expansion forces.

Under this sign convention (the standard IUPAC convention), heat added to the system () and work done on the system () increase its internal energy.

3. Differential Form

When focusing strictly on the system, the “” subscript is dropped for simplicity.

Expressed for an infinitesimal process:

is an exact differential, indicating that internal energy is a state function (depends only on the current state, not the path taken).

If we limit to boundary work:

Note

Physical meaning. Represents mechanical expansion or compression work exerted across a movable system boundary (such as a piston).

Sign convention.

  • When a system expands (), it does work on the surroundings, spending its own internal energy; hence .
  • When a system is compressed (), the surroundings do work on the system, adding energy; hence .
  • The negative sign ensures consistency with the standard IUPAC convention where energy entering the system is positive.

Note

Substituting into limits the mechanical interactions strictly to reversible boundary work, neglecting other forms like shaft work, electrical work, or surface tension.

Internal energy therefore changes through two primary pathways: heat transfer () and mechanical volume changes ().

4. Extension to Variable Composition and Open Systems

4.1. Functional Dependence of Internal Energy

For a closed system of fixed composition, internal energy depends only on two independent extensive state variables—typically entropy and volume :

If matter can cross the boundary, or if chemical reactions/phase changes alter the amounts of species present, must also depend explicitly on the mole numbers of each constituent species :

4.2. Total Differential via Multivariable Calculus

Taking the total differential of using the chain rule gives:

4.3. Definition of Chemical Potential

The partial derivative with respect to composition is defined as the chemical potential of species :

Substituting these definitions into the total differential yields:

Note

Physical reason. If molecules are added to or removed from a system, they carry internal energy with them (chemical bond energies, rotational/vibrational modes, and intermolecular potential energy with neighboring molecules). Even if heat transfer is zero () and the volume remains rigid (), adding particles changes the total internal energy of the system. The summation term directly tracks that energetic change.

5. The Second Law

The Second Law of Thermodynamics is often more conceptually challenging for students than the First Law. At its core, the Second Law can be summarized simply: the total entropy of the universe can never decrease.

While the First Law focuses on the conservation of energy, the Second Law dictates the direction of natural processes. For example, the First Law alone doesn’t rule out liquid water spontaneously freezing above its melting temperature; it only dictates the energy balance if such a process occurred. By introducing an inequality, the Second Law expressly forbids certain processes, establishing what is physically possible.

It is important to note that the Second Law does not prevent the entropy of a specific system or its surroundings from decreasing individually—it only requires that their combined total cannot decrease. Furthermore, to make this principle practical, we need a way to actually calculate entropy changes. This is where the concept of a reversible process is introduced. In a purely reversible process, the total entropy change of the universe (system plus surroundings) is exactly zero, turning the inequality of Eq. 7 into an equality. This allows us to define the differential change in entropy mathematically as:

6. Why State Functions, Not Path Functions

By combining the First and Second Laws of Thermodynamics, we replace path functions (Q, W) with exact differentials (state functions: Internal Energy, Temperature, Entropy, Pressure, and Volume) to create the Fundamental Thermodynamic Relation (Equation 6).

Path functions are not practically “bad”—in fact, heat and work are exactly what engineers care about because that is what we pay for in the real world (e.g., fuel for heat, electricity for work). However, from a mathematical and analytical standpoint, path functions are incredibly difficult to work with compared to state functions for three main reasons:

6.1. The “Memory” Problem

To calculate a path function like work (), you cannot just look at the starting and ending volumes. You must know the exact history of how the expansion happened. Did the pressure drop linearly? Exponentially? Was there friction? Was it done infinitely slowly (reversible) or violently (irreversible)? If you do not know the exact mathematical function of the path taken, you cannot solve the integral.

State functions, however, have no memory. To find the change in internal energy (), you only need simple subtraction: . You do not need to know anything about the process itself.

6.2. You Cannot Put Path Functions in a Table

Because state functions () only depend on the current physical condition of the system, we can tabulate them. This is why we have Steam Tables and thermodynamic databases (like CoolProp or NIST). You can look up the exact internal energy or entropy of water at and .

You can never create a table for “Heat” or “Work” because a system does not contain heat or work. They are actions, not properties.

6.3. The Thermodynamic “Cheat Code”

Real-world processes are almost always irreversible (they happen quickly, with friction, turbulence, and heat loss). Calculating or for an irreversible process is mathematically messy, sometimes impossible.

Because state functions only care about the endpoints, they unlock a massive analytical loophole: You can calculate the change for a chaotic, irreversible process by inventing an imaginary, perfectly reversible path between the same two states.

  • If you want to know for a messy explosion in a cylinder, you don’t need to model the explosion’s path.
  • You just look at the state before the explosion () and the state after the explosion ().
  • You use the fundamental relation () over an easy, idealized path to find the difference between those two states.
  • Because is a state function, the you calculate for the imaginary easy path is 100% identical to the of the messy real-world explosion.
